extracted.intended_audience: children's librarians, library professionals, authors/illustrators and others interested in the Carnegie and Kate Greenaway awards
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive guidance and historical notes about the CILIP Carnegie and Kate Greenaway Medals, their purposes, who may nominate and judge, and values emphasised (writing, illustration, diversity, engagement). Useful for librarians, judges, entrants and observers of these UK children’s book awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognising outstanding writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The CILIP Carnegie Medal is awarded by children’s librarians for an outstanding book written in English for children and young people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Medal recognises 'outstanding writing' in books for children and young people; award decisions are made by children's librarians and reflect a long-standing aim to celebrate excellence in writing for young readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognising outstanding illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: The CILIP Kate Greenaway Medal recognises outstanding illustration in books for children and young people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration is judged as a separate dimension of excellence; the Kate Greenaway Medal (and associated honours) specifically reward illustrators' achievement in children's books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work must be written in English (Carnegie)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Carnegie Medal is awarded for an outstanding book written in English for children and young people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This language requirement is stated explicitly as part of the eligibility for the Carnegie Medal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominations submitted by librarians
rubrics_metrics.description: The selected books for consideration would be nominated by librarians, a practice which continues to this day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry/consideration is gatekept by librarians' nominations rather than open submission; this shapes the longlist/shortlist and reflects professional curation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judging by children's librarians with direct experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The Medal was originally judged by a small team of senior members of the Library Association, but after criticism the panel was changed to include librarians specialising in children’s services so that judges work directly with children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges are expected to be practitioners who understand children's readership; later reforms added branch representatives and regional judges to broaden representation on panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate excellence and raise standards in children's literature
rubrics_metrics.description: The Medal was introduced 'in order to “raise the level of children’s literature after the golden age of the Edwardian period”.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A foundational remit of the award is to promote higher standards in writing/illustration for children, so judges historically and presently are guided by that improvement/celebration imperative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to diversity and celebrating lived experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The award, while celebrating excellence, is 'forging ahead into the 21st century with a commitment to diversity and celebrating lived experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent judging ethos explicitly values diversity of voices and authentic representation of lived experience among shortlisted and winning works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children’s literature as 'mirror and window' — representation and empowerment
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Children’s literature should be a mirror and a window.' Works should allow readers to 'see one’s own experience and community reflected' and to explore other worlds and perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges prize books that both reflect readers' lives (representation) and open imaginative possibilities; linked to the rights of the child to education and to access reading that resonates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of human-rights themes (Amnesty Honour)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2016 a new award, the Amnesty Honour, was introduced to recognise the theme of human rights in the shortlisted titles; the Kate Greenaway Amnesty Honour (for illustration in a children’s book) is judged by Amnesty UK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplemental honour highlights human-rights content as an evaluative axis and involves external expert judging (Amnesty UK) for that theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with young readers via shadowing initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The medal’s shadowing initiative and related activity engage young readers and provoke discussion and debate around shortlisted works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shadowing (young reader participation alongside official judging) is presented as a valued mechanism for assessing a book’s impact on its intended audience and fostering public engagement with the award.
